967.title: Across the Sahara
967.hook: Muslim traders cross the desert with salt, gold and books
967.howItsDone: Muslims in West Africa often tell the story of their faith arriving with traders and teachers who crossed the Sahara, and old trading towns at the desert's edge are still remembered as places of learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Misr, Egypt and the Nile, a land whose faith changed without a single dramatic day. Your line was slowly, over centuries.

A town built of salt. The walls of the houses are salt blocks, the roofs are camel skins, and the mosque is made of salt as well. Nothing grows there; the people live on dates and grain carried in from far away. The traveler Ibn Battuta stopped at this place, Taghaza, in the middle of the Sahara, and wrote it down. He was heading south with a caravan, toward the lands along the Niger River. Salt was going south. Gold was coming north. And riding with the camels, quieter than either, came something else. Today: across the Sahara.
screen: `A TOWN BUILT OF SALT.` → `A MOSQUE OF SALT BLOCKS.` → `A CARAVAN HEADING SOUTH.`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ grew up among the merchants of Mecca, and the Qur'an speaks of the caravans of his tribe, Quraysh, setting out in winter and in summer. Commentators connect one verse to pilgrims who wondered whether they could buy and sell on the road to Hajj. In Pickthall's translation: "It is no sin for you that ye seek the bounty of your Lord (by trading)." A merchant and a believer could be the same person, praying at the side of a camel. Islam crossed the Sahara along these trade roads, with merchants and teachers. A caravan was a moving village. It traveled together, stopped together at the times of prayer, and lived or died by trust. Ibn Battuta describes how his caravan paid one man to ride ahead alone to the next town, so its people could carry water out to meet the travelers. If that rider got lost, everyone was in danger. Salt from the desert went south. Gold from West Africa went north, to the cities of the Mediterranean. And alongside both traveled scholars, copies of the Qur'an, books of law, grammar and prayer. A merchant who settled in a town south of the desert needed a mosque, a teacher for his children, a judge for his contracts. So the towns at the desert's edge became places of learning as well as markets. The salt was eaten. The gold was spent. The books stayed, and were copied, and were taught.
screen: `THE QUR'AN AND THE CARAVAN.` · `A MOVING VILLAGE THAT RUNS ON TRUST.` · `SALT SOUTH, GOLD NORTH.` · `BOOKS STAY, AND ARE TAUGHT.` · then, large: `SALT, GOLD AND BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind who has a long road ahead: a new job, a hard winter, an exam, a first year away from home. Look along your own shelf, in your mind, for the book that would travel well with them, a Qur'an, a book of prayers, a novel, a book that got you through something. If you pray, hold that person before God; if not, keep them in mind and think about which book, and why.
Across the Sahara. The desert trade roads, where salt went south, gold went north, and Islam traveled with the caravans. Today's word.
Your line: salt, gold and books. A caravan lived or died by trust. See you tomorrow.

968.title: The empire of Mali
968.hook: the Mali empire grows rich on trade, with Muslim kings and scholars
968.howItsDone: In Mali and across West Africa, griots still sing the epic of Sundiata, and Muslims there remember the old empire's mosques and scholars as part of their own history.

segments.voice: Yesterday: across the Sahara, with a town of salt and a caravan that ran on trust. Your line was salt, gold and books.

Friday, in the capital of a West African king. Get to the mosque late and there's no room left to pray, so people send servants ahead early in the morning with prayer mats, to spread them out and hold a place. A visitor from Morocco wrote it down: Ibn Battuta again, now at the court of the mansa, the king of Mali. He had complaints. The welcome gift the king sent him, a little bread, some meat and some yogurt, struck him as far too small, and he said so. But on other things he wrote with open admiration. Today: the empire of Mali.
screen: `FRIDAY: NO ROOM LEFT TO PRAY.` → `PRAYER MATS SENT AHEAD.` → `A VISITOR AT THE MANSA'S COURT.`

segments.voice: Mali grew along the Niger River, close to the gold fields of West Africa, where the trade roads from the desert came down to the water. Its people remember the empire's founder through the epic of Sundiata, a story sung by griots, the keepers of history in song. Its kings were Muslim, and the court held both worlds at once: Ibn Battuta saw the griots performing before the king, and he saw the judge and the preachers of the mosque. What impressed him? First, safety: a traveler in Mali, he wrote, had no need to fear robbers on the road. Second, honesty with the dead. When a stranger died in the country, his goods were not seized; they were kept in trust until the rightful heir came to claim them. Third, care for prayer: the crowded Fridays, the clean white clothes. And fourth, care for the Qur'an, which children were made to learn by heart. That second point echoes a verse. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners, and, if ye judge between mankind, that ye judge justly." A dead stranger's goods are a hard deposit to return, because nobody is watching. Ibn Battuta noticed. Gold made Mali rich. What a traveler remembered was whether his bags, and his life, were safe on its roads.

969.title: Mansa Musa's Hajj
969.hook: Mali's king travels to Mecca with so much gold that Cairo's prices fall
969.howItsDone: Muslims who are able are called to make the Hajj to Mecca, and the Qur'an's call to spend in charity travels with them. In West Africa, Mansa Musa's pilgrimage is still told as part of Mali's history.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the empire of Mali, with safe roads and a dead stranger's goods kept for his heir. Your line was safe on its roads.

Cairo, the palace of the sultan of Egypt. A visiting king from West Africa is brought in, and the courtiers tell him what everyone does here: kiss the ground before the sultan. He refuses. He has come as a pilgrim, on his way to Mecca, and he won't bow to a man. The room goes tense. Then someone beside him whispers a word, and the visitor speaks: he bows, he says, to God who created him. And he goes down in prostration. The sultan lets it pass, and treats him with honor. The Cairo writer al-Umari heard the story from people who were there. Today: Mansa Musa's Hajj.
screen: `A KING AT THE SULTAN'S COURT.` → `HE WON'T BOW TO A MAN.` → `I BOW TO GOD WHO CREATED ME.`

segments.voice: Hajj is not optional for a Muslim who can manage it. In Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an: "And pilgrimage to the House is a duty unto Allah for mankind, for him who can find a way thither." Mansa Musa, king of Mali, could find a way. He crossed the desert with a great company of people and a great deal of gold, and he did not keep it to himself. In Cairo he spent and gave so freely, al-Umari reports, that gold lost its value in the city, and people there were still talking about it years later. Turn that around for a moment: a man gave away so much that the price of the thing he gave fell. Then the ending. On the way home, al-Umari says, Mansa Musa ran short and had to borrow from the merchants of Cairo. The king of gold, in debt at the end of his pilgrimage. Some call him the richest pilgrim. Nobody can really count his gold. What the sources describe is something else: a pilgrim who refused to bow to a sultan, bowed to God instead, gave without counting, and came home with less. After the Hajj, tradition says, Mali's name traveled north to the cities of the Mediterranean, and scholars and builders traveled back with him. Generosity, here, was not a side detail. It was the story.
screen: `A DUTY FOR WHOEVER CAN FIND A WAY.` · `SO MUCH GOLD THAT ITS VALUE FELL.` · `THE KING BORROWS TO GET HOME.` · `MALI'S NAME TRAVELS NORTH.` · then, large: `THE RICHEST PILGRIM.`

segments.voice: Generosity doesn't need gold; it needs something you'd rather keep: your time, your attention, money, praise, the last of something good. 970.title: Timbuktu's manuscripts
970.hook: a city of scholars, with the Sankore mosque and its manuscripts kept in family libraries
970.howItsDone: Families and libraries in Timbuktu still keep manuscripts, and scholars and conservators work to preserve, catalog and photograph them so they can be read.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mansa Musa's Hajj, a king who gave so much that gold lost its value, and borrowed to get home. Your line was the richest pilgrim.

In English, "from here to Timbuktu" means the end of the earth, a place so far away it might as well be invented. But Timbuktu is real. It sits near the bend of the Niger, at the edge of the desert. In its mud-brick houses, families kept wooden chests and cupboards full of handwritten books, some pages brittle and brown, with notes squeezed into the margins. A traveler known as Leo Africanus passed through and noticed something strange about the market: books were among the most valuable things for sale. Today: Timbuktu's manuscripts.
screen: `THE END OF THE EARTH?` → `A REAL TOWN ON THE NIGER.` → `CHESTS FULL OF HANDWRITTEN BOOKS.`

segments.voice: One surah of the Qur'an, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, is named al-Qalam, the Pen, and it opens with an oath. In Pickthall's translation: "Nun. By the pen and that which they write (therein)." Timbuktu took the pen seriously. Leo Africanus wrote that the town had many judges, teachers and learned men, paid by the king, and that handwritten books brought from North Africa sold there for more than any other merchandise. Scholars gathered at mosques like Sankore, and students sat with teachers one book at a time, often copying the book for themselves as they studied it. What's in the manuscripts? Copies of the Qur'an, yes. But also law, grammar, the life of the Prophet, Sufi poetry, astronomy for setting prayer times, medicine, letters between scholars, records of sales and debts and marriages. A whole town's mind, written down. The chronicler al-Sa'di remembers the scholar Ahmad Baba, who was carried away from Timbuktu into exile after Moroccan forces took the city. Tradition says he mourned the books he lost. Families kept the rest, generation after generation, and tradition says some were hidden in walls or buried in the sand. And in recent years, when armed men held the town, librarians and families carried manuscripts away to safety in trunks. Gold passed through Timbuktu. The pages stayed.

segments.voice: Go back over what the chests held: law, grammar, the life of the Prophet, poetry, the stars, medicine, letters, records of debts and marriages, and let one of them catch your interest. 971.title: The mud mosque of Djenné
971.hook: the Great Mosque of mud, replastered by the whole town
971.howItsDone: In Djenné the townspeople gather for the replastering of the Great Mosque, led by the masons, with young people carrying mud and others bringing water.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Timbuktu's manuscripts, books that sold for more than other goods in the market. Your line was the city of manuscripts.

Before dawn, drums. Then people pour into the square: boys with baskets of wet mud on their heads, women and girls carrying water from the river, old men giving orders, masons up on the walls. Bundles of palm wood stick out of the building like the bristles of a brush, and men climb them like ladders, smoothing fresh mud over the walls with their hands. By the end of the day a whole mosque has a new skin. This is Djenné, an old town on a river in Mali, and its Great Mosque is built of earth. Today: the mud mosque of Djenné.
screen: `DRUMS BEFORE DAWN.` → `BASKETS OF WET MUD.` → `A WHOLE MOSQUE GETS A NEW SKIN.`

segments.voice: Mud is a strange thing to build a great mosque from: sun-dried bricks, held together and coated with more mud, mixed with things like rice husks so it holds. It is cool inside in the heat. But mud has an enemy: rain. The rainy season washes some of the walls away. So, by long custom, the town comes out together and puts it back. The masons lead; their skill is handed down in families. Everyone else carries. Those palm sticks poking out of the walls aren't decoration. They're scaffolding that never comes down. The chronicler al-Sa'di tells how the town's first mosque came to be: a ruler of Djenné became Muslim, tore down his own palace, and built a mosque on the site. The building that stands today is not that first one, but it stands in its line. The Qur'an has a line about who looks after the houses of God. In Pickthall's translation: "He only shall tend Allah's sanctuaries who believeth in Allah and the Last Day." And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that whoever builds a mosque for God, God builds the like of it for them in Paradise. In Djenné, building is never finished. The mosque would melt without the town, and the town gathers because of the mosque. Nobody owns the job. Everyone owns a basket.

972.title: The Songhay empire
972.hook: Askia Muhammad's empire and his Hajj
972.howItsDone: Historians and Muslims in the Sahel read the Timbuktu chronicles and al-Maghili's replies to Askia Muhammad to understand how Songhay's rulers and scholars worked together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mud mosque of Djenné, renewed after the rains. Your line was the whole town replasters.

A ruler holds a huge stretch of the Niger valley: armies, towns, river fleets, taxes coming in. And what does he do? He sits down and writes questions to a scholar. How should a Muslim ruler treat people who pray but still keep the old idols? What do I do about judges who take bribes? When is it right to take someone's property, and when is it theft? The scholar, al-Maghili, wrote back, and his answers were kept. The ruler was Askia Muhammad. Today: the Songhay empire.
screen: `POWER OVER THE NIGER VALLEY.` → `A RULER WRITES QUESTIONS.` → `A SCHOLAR WRITES BACK.`

segments.voice: Songhay grew up along the Niger, the river people of Gao, and in time its rulers took over towns that had once looked to Mali: Timbuktu, Djenné, the markets of the river bend. The chronicles of Timbuktu, the Ta'rikh al-Sudan and the Ta'rikh al-Fattash, tell the story from the scholars' side. One ruler, Sunni Ali, was a great conqueror, and the chronicles remember him harshly, as a man who mistreated the scholars of Timbuktu. After his death, one of his commanders, Muhammad, took power and became the askia, the title of the new line of kings. The chronicles remember him very differently. He kept scholars close, appointed judges, and asked questions. And he made the Hajj. The Qur'an pictures pilgrims arriving from everywhere. In Pickthall's translation: "They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine." Askia Muhammad came from very far. The chronicles say he gave generously in the holy cities, and that on this journey he was named a khalifa, a deputy, over the lands of West Africa, though they differ on who named him. He came home with a title that tied his rule to something larger than his own armies. His story asks a quiet question: what makes power legitimate? For him, part of the answer was going a long way to stand among other pilgrims, and part was being willing to ask a scholar how to rule well.

segments.voice: A pilgrimage is a journey made not for business or holiday but to stand somewhere that matters: some Muslims long for Hajj for years, others make smaller journeys, to a grave, a mosque, a teacher. Let a place your feet have taken you for a reason like that, or a place you hope they will, come to mind, and stay with it. If you pray, ask God for the way to get there; if not, simply hold the place in mind.

973.title: The Swahili coast
973.hook: Kilwa, Lamu and Zanzibar, stone towns of Muslim traders on the Indian Ocean
973.howItsDone: Muslims on the Swahili coast pray in old coral-stone mosques in towns like Lamu and Zanzibar, and Swahili is spoken across East Africa.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Songhay empire, and a ruler who wrote his questions to a scholar. Your line was the askia.

A poor man walks up to the sultan of Kilwa after Friday prayer and asks him for the clothes he is wearing. Not money. The clothes. The sultan doesn't laugh him off. He goes home, changes, and gives the man the very clothes off his back. Ibn Battuta was in the town and tells the story, and says the sultan was known for his giving. Kilwa is on the other side of Africa from everything this week: not the desert, but the Indian Ocean coast, among towns where the sea, not the sand, carried everything in. Today: the Swahili coast.
screen: `ASKED FOR THE CLOTHES OFF HIS BACK.` → `THE SULTAN GIVES THEM.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF AFRICA.`

segments.voice: Along Africa's east coast, from what is now Somalia down toward Mozambique, Muslim trading towns grew up on islands and inlets: Kilwa, Mombasa, Lamu, Zanzibar, and more. They were built of coral stone cut from the reef, with carved wooden doors and mosques by the water. Ibn Battuta called Kilwa one of the most beautiful and well-built towns he had seen. What made these towns possible was the wind. The monsoon blows one way for part of the year and the other way for the rest. Ships from Arabia, Persia and India rode it down to Africa, waited for the wind to turn, and rode it home. In the waiting, traders stayed. They married into local families, prayed in local mosques, and a coastal Muslim culture grew, with its own language, Swahili, an African language rich in words borrowed from Arabic. The Qur'an counts the winds and the ships among God's signs: it speaks of winds sent as bearers of good news, so that the ships may sail by God's command and people may seek His bounty. On this coast, that was simply the shape of the year. So ends one week: the Sahara's salt, gold and books; the empire of Mali; Mansa Musa's Hajj; Timbuktu's manuscripts; Djenné's mud mosque; Songhay's askia; and now the coast, where faith arrived by sea.
screen: `STONE TOWNS ON ISLANDS AND INLETS.` · `THE MONSOON TURNS, THE SHIPS WAIT.` · `TRADERS STAY, A LANGUAGE GROWS.` · `ONE WEEK, DESERT TO SEA.` · then, large: `TOWNS OF THE MONSOON.`

segments.voice: Picture a map: the east coast of Africa, then the Arabian Peninsula, then India, and trace a line across the water between them and back again, one trader's year, out with one wind and home with the other. Breathe in as you trace out, and out as you trace back. If you pray, remember those who traveled that water and prayed on its shores; if not, simply feel the rhythm of going and returning.
Swahili. The language and culture that grew along Africa's Indian Ocean coast, from Kilwa to Lamu and Zanzibar, whose year turned with the monsoon wind. Today's word.
Your line: towns of the monsoon. Out with one wind, home with the other. Day nine hundred seventy-three.
